explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. David says it plainly: "for in You my soul takes refuge." He's in a cave with a king after him, and he still points straight at God. When I was stuck in that drawer, I would have taken any refuge going, so I admire a man who picks the best one.

Good guess, friend, but not here. Psalm 57:1 never mentions Jonathan. David says, "in You my soul takes refuge," and the "You" is God, since he opens with "Have mercy on me, O God." Cave hide-outs are crowded with names, but only one gets the refuge.

I get why you'd think so, baker. Anybody running for their life might lean on the folks around them. But the psalm doesn't say that. David says, "for in You my soul takes refuge," and he's talking to God, right after crying, "Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy."

Right on the money, baker. David says, "In the shadow of Your wings I will take shelter until the danger has passed." Notice he doesn't say he's leaving early. He settles in and stays under there till the trouble is done. That's a man who knows where the good shade is.
Nice thought, friend, but David never mentions the sun here. He says he'll take shelter "until the danger has passed." So the clock isn't the thing. The danger is, and he stays put until it's gone.

That sounds reasonable, doesn't it? But the psalm doesn't say a word about David's strength. He says, "I will take shelter until the danger has passed." The shelter stays until the trouble is over, whatever shape he's in.

Yes, baker! David cries out "to God Most High, to God who fulfills His purpose for me." Even from a cave, he's sure God has a purpose for him and will carry it out. That's a lot of confidence for a man hiding from a king.

Close in spirit, friend, but that's not what he says. David says God "fulfills His purpose for me." Nothing in verse 2 says God hands him a map of every step. Honestly, I'd take the purpose over the map any day.
Ooh, that would've ended the cave days quick, wouldn't it? But Psalm 57:2 says nothing about a throne. David says God "fulfills His purpose for me." The psalm leaves it right there, so I will too.
Not quite, baker, and I'm glad it's not. David says, "He reaches down from heaven and saves me." God doesn't sit up there and let him wait it out alone. He reaches down.

That's right, friend. David says, "He reaches down from heaven and saves me." God isn't stuck up in heaven watching from a distance. In the cave, David says God reaches down and rebukes those who trample him.

explanations.answer: His loving devotion and His truth
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. David says, "God sends forth His loving devotion and His truth." Right after talking about enemies, he talks about what God sends. I think that's a pretty good reply to trouble.

I see why you'd pick it, friend, since the verse just mentioned God rebuking those who trample David. But the verse says, "God sends forth His loving devotion and His truth." Anger and judgment don't show up in that line at all.
Dramatic choice, baker! It sounds like a movie trailer. But Psalm 57:3 says, "God sends forth His loving devotion and His truth." No fire, no storm. Just devotion and truth.

Yes, baker. David says he lies down "with men whose teeth are spears and arrows, whose tongues are sharp swords." Those are his words for how sharp and cutting these men are. I think that's the toughest crowd you could share a cave with.
Big guess, friend, but no giants in this psalm. David says he lies down with "men whose teeth are spears and arrows, whose tongues are sharp swords." The word in the verse is simply men.
Spooky pick, baker, but that's not what David says. He says the beasts are "men whose teeth are spears and arrows, whose tongues are sharp swords." Real men, with words that cut like blades.

That's it, baker! Right in the middle of the lions, David says, "Be exalted, O God, above the heavens; may Your glory cover all the earth." He doesn't ask for his own safety there. He lifts his eyes to God's glory. That's some focus.

explanations.answer: Strike down the men around me
explanations.explanation: I can see the temptation, friend, with those spear-teeth around. But that's not what David says in verse 5. He says, "Be exalted, O God, above the heavens; may Your glory cover all the earth." His words here are about God's glory.

explanations.answer: Keep this cave hidden from Saul
explanations.explanation: Makes sense for a man in a cave, baker. But David doesn't ask that in verse 5. He says, "Be exalted, O God, above the heavens; may Your glory cover all the earth." He's talking about God's glory.
Yes, baker. David says, "They dug a pit before me, but they themselves have fallen into it!" The pit they dug for him caught them instead. I think that's a plot twist worth a Selah.
Not this time, friend. David says, "They dug a pit before me, but they themselves have fallen into it!" So the pit they dug ended up swallowing them, not him.

That's right, baker! David says, "My heart is steadfast, O God, my heart is steadfast. I will sing and make music." A cave, a king hunting him, and he's planning a concert. I'd still be checking the cave for exits.
Reasonable for a hiding man, friend, but David says otherwise. He says, "I will sing and make music." Not a quiet word in the plan.
Ha, that's what my feet would vote for, baker. But David doesn't say that. With his heart steadfast, he says, "I will sing and make music."
Yes, baker. David says, "Awake, my glory! Awake, O harp and lyre!" He's talking to his instruments like they're sleeping in. I wish somebody would talk to my oven that way.
Not quite, friend. In Psalm 57:8 David says, "Awake, my glory! Awake, O harp and lyre!" He really does call on the harp and lyre to wake up, and then he adds, "I will awaken the dawn."
Not this time, baker. David says, "I will praise You, O Lord, among the nations; I will sing Your praises among the peoples." That's about as far from private as it gets.

Right, friend. David says, "I will praise You, O Lord, among the nations; I will sing Your praises among the peoples." He's not keeping this song in the cave. He plans to sing it out loud among the nations.
That's right, baker. David says, "For Your loving devotion reaches to the heavens, and Your faithfulness to the clouds." That's his reason for singing among the peoples. Pretty high, friend.
Good height, baker, but not high enough. David says, "Your loving devotion reaches to the heavens." Mountaintops don't come up in verse 10.
That's aiming a little low, friend! David says, "For Your loving devotion reaches to the heavens." Treetops never come up in Psalm 57:10.
